title: Just Let Them Play | A Game's First 3 Minutes, Through Super Mario Odyssey

scenes.title: Press Start, and You're Already Mario
lines: Ever started a new game, pressed Start, and found yourself still watching a cutscene minutes later? Your hands are ready but there's nothing to do, and that time feels longer than it is.
Players don't judge fun by hearing it explained. They try it and decide. That's why how quickly a game lets people play in the first few minutes matters.
Super Mario Odyssey handles this very quickly. After a short opening, Mario lands in the Cap Kingdom, and from there the running and jumping are in the player's hands.
The first prompts after the opening are simple too: look around, run, jump. That is all.
Today, let's take apart how Odyssey's first few minutes are ordered, one system at a time.

scenes.title: A Game Explained by One Cap
lines: The first thing you get after taking control is the cap throw.
Throw it and coins pop and crates break; throw it at an enemy and you become that enemy. One button carries many uses.
So after a few seconds you can tell what this game is about: throw, break, take over.
Breaking crates and pulling back a Chain Chomp to launch it both start from the same cap. Instead of memorizing new buttons, you discover new uses for an action you already know.
When the core action is gathered into one, there's only one thing to learn at first. The rest grows naturally as you use that action in more places.

scenes.title: Keep the Story Short, Start in the Middle
lines: So what about the story? Odyssey's opening starts on an airship where a fight is already underway.
It doesn't spend long on why Bowser wants a wedding or why the two are fighting. That part is a short cutscene, not gameplay, but it drops you straight into the action.
Instead of stacking backstory up front, it shows only what's happening and moves straight on to play.
It's fine if the player doesn't know what's going on yet. Once it's in their hands, the urge to find out actually carries the story forward.
Keep the story, but pull the controls forward. That's the order of Odyssey's first scene.

scenes.title: Not Watching, Becoming
lines: Why put play this far forward?
Films and animation can show great visuals and stories too. But a character moving when you press a button, and a world reacting to you, is something only games can offer.
In the Cascade Kingdom, throw your cap at a dinosaur and now you are the dinosaur, smashing through whatever blocked the way. That's a feel you can't get just by watching.
The moment you become the dinosaur, your size, your movement and what you can break all change at once. Hearing that explained and steering it yourself are completely different experiences.
Let players taste that feel in the first few minutes, and they'll figure out for themselves what they'll be doing in this game.

scenes.title: Tutorial and Title Come After Play
lines: The tutorial works the same way. The Cap Kingdom doesn't set aside practice for cap throws and captures; it lets you use them right on the main path.
Throw your cap at a frog and you can jump high, and that height opens the next path. The moment you learn is already the real game.
Here's a fun detail: when you start a new game, the Super Mario Odyssey title sequence only appears after you beat the first boss. Play comes before the title.
A short opening, a core action gathered into one cap, a tutorial inside the main game, a title that follows play. That order makes Odyssey's first few minutes.
Try timing your own game's first three minutes. After pressing Start, when does the player first move, and does that movement tell them why the game is fun?
Don't make them wait. Let them play first.
